domain_restrictions: A,B,d are integers with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0
Empty product convention: if d=0 then ∏_{i=1}^0 (...) = 1 so Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1
Assumption: the rational expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) is actually a polynomial, i.e., Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q] (not just a rational function)
Graded ring S is Q[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=B+i for i=1..d
If d=0, interpret S as Q (no variables, hence no f_i witnesses needed)
Each f_i is homogeneous in S with weighted degree deg(f_i)=A+i
Regularity condition: in the successive quotient S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}), the class of f_i is not a zero-divisor (equivalently: (f_1,...,f_d) is a homogeneous regular sequence in S)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let A,B,d ∈ Z with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q_{A,B,d}(q)=∏_{i=1}^d (1-q^{A+i})/(1-q^{B+i}) with Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1. If Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q], then in the weighted graded polynomial ring S=Q[x_1,...,x_d] (or S=Q if d=0) with deg(x_i)=B+i, there exist homogeneous elements f_1,...,f_d ∈ S such that deg(f_i)=A+i for each i=1..d and for each i the class of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor (so f_1,...,f_d form a homogeneous regular sequence). Consequently, the graded data of S modulo this regular sequence yields the given expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) (as stated in the equivalence).

Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) := ∏_{i=1}^d (1-q^{A+i})/(1-q^{B+i}) belongs to Q[q] (q formal indeterminate)
There exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that for each i=1..d: deg(f_i)=A+i, and the image of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.proof_nl:
First suppose d = 0. Then S = k. The only ideals of S are 0 and S. Affine 0-space over an algebraic closure has exactly one point, namely the empty tuple, so the zero locus of 0 is that point and the zero locus of S is empty. Since the zero locus of I is assumed to be exactly the origin, we must have I = 0. Hence S/I = k, which is finite-dimensional over k.

Now assume d >= 1. Let kbar be an algebraic closure of k, let T = kbar[x_1, ..., x_d], and let J = IT be the ideal of T generated by I. The common zero set of J in kbar^d is the same as that of I: indeed, if a in kbar^d satisfies g(a) = 0 for every g in I, then every element of J, being a finite sum of terms u g with u in T and g in I, also vanishes at a; the converse is immediate from I subseteq J. Thus V(J) = {(0, ..., 0)}.

Subclaim 1: for each i there exists N_i >= 1 such that x_i^(N_i) lies in J.

Proof of Subclaim 1. In T, the ideal of all polynomials vanishing at the origin is exactly m = (x_1, ..., x_d), because a polynomial vanishes at the origin if and only if its constant term is 0. Since V(J) = {(0, ..., 0)}, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz over the algebraically closed field kbar gives
sqrt(J) = I(V(J)) = m.
Therefore x_i lies in sqrt(J) for every i, so by definition of radical there exists N_i >= 1 with x_i^(N_i) in J. This proves the subclaim.

Subclaim 2: J intersect S = I.

Proof of Subclaim 2. The inclusion I subseteq J intersect S is clear. For the reverse inclusion, take f in J intersect S. Then
f = sum_{nu=1}^r u_nu g_nu
for some g_nu in I and u_nu in T. Let W be the k-subspace of kbar spanned by 1 and by all coefficients appearing in the finitely many polynomials u_nu. Choose a k-basis e_1 = 1, e_2, ..., e_m of W. Write
u_nu = sum_{j=1}^m e_j h_{nu,j}
with h_{nu,j} in S. Then
f = sum_{j=1}^m e_j F_j,
where F_j := sum_{nu=1}^r h_{nu,j} g_nu belongs to I.

If sum_{j=1}^m e_j P_j = 0 with P_j in S, then comparing the coefficient of each monomial gives a k-linear relation among e_1, ..., e_m; since they are k-linearly independent, every coefficient in every P_j is 0, hence each P_j = 0. So such an expression is unique.

But f itself lies in S, so also
f = e_1 f + sum_{j=2}^m e_j 0.
By uniqueness, F_1 = f and F_j = 0 for j >= 2. In particular f lies in I. Thus J intersect S = I, proving the subclaim.

Now Subclaim 1 gives x_i^(N_i) in J for each i, and Subclaim 2 then implies x_i^(N_i) in I for each i. Hence every monomial x_1^(a_1) ... x_d^(a_d) with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, because it is divisible by x_i^(N_i). Therefore every class in S/I is represented by a k-linear combination of the finitely many monomials x_1^(a_1) ... x_d^(a_d) with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i. These finitely many classes span S/I over k.

So S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

payload.statement_nl: Let k be a field, let d be a nonnegative integer, let w_1,...,w_d be positive integers, and let S = k[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=w_i. Let I be a homogeneous ideal of S. If, over an algebraic closure of k, the common zero locus of I in affine d-space is exactly the origin, then S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

dependency_assessment.notes: No forbidden ancestry claims are used. The only substantial external input is Nullstellensatz, invoked explicitly in the proof.

detailed_findings.finding: The main argument is correct: from V(J) = {(0,...,0)}, Nullstellensatz gives sqrt(J) = (x_1,...,x_d), hence x_i^N_i ∈ J for each i.
The proof of J ∩ S = I is valid via expansion of coefficients in a finite k-basis of their span inside kbar.
Once x_i^N_i ∈ I for all i, the bounded-exponent monomials indeed span S/I, establishing finite-dimensionality.
The proof does not use the homogeneity of I or the weights w_i; this is harmless because the argument establishes a stronger statement.

result_payload.reason: The proof is mathematically complete and uses a standard correct strategy: pass to the algebraic closure, extend the ideal, apply Nullstellensatz to show each variable is nilpotent modulo the extended ideal, prove contraction J ∩ S = I, and conclude that S/I is spanned by finitely many bounded-exponent monomials. The d = 0 case is handled separately and correctly. The argument proves a slightly stronger statement than stated, since homogeneity and the weights are not needed, but this is not semantic drift.
